practice.title: Estimate a chat app
practice.brief: Paper/markdown only. Estimate peak QPS, daily storage and 1-year storage for a chat app with 1M DAU, 20 messages/user/day, 200-byte messages, 3x peak factor, messages kept 1 year. Then write its API (3-5 endpoints) and core entities.
practice.done_when: ESTIMATE.md shows every multiplication with units, arrives at ~230 avg / ~700 peak write QPS and ~1.5 TB/yr raw (or justifies different assumptions), and lists the API before any database is named.

quiz.prompt: 1M DAU x 20 requests/day is roughly what average QPS?
quiz.explain: 20,000,000 / 86,400 s ~= 231 requests per second on average; peak is a multiple of that.

quiz.prompt: 'p99 latency < 200 ms' is a:
quiz.explain: It constrains how well the system performs, not what it does.

quiz.prompt: The first step in a design interview is to:

quiz.prompt: Why design the API and core entities before choosing storage?
rubric: Access patterns (reads/writes, queries) come from the API and drive storage choice.
Avoids premature technology choices; keeps the design requirement-driven.

practice.title: Two replicas behind nginx

quiz.prompt: An L7 load balancer can route by:
quiz.explain: L7 understands HTTP; L4 only sees IPs/ports.

quiz.prompt: Horizontal scaling is easiest when servers are:
quiz.explain: Any replica can serve any request when state lives in shared stores.

quiz.prompt: Streaming LLM tokens to a browser most simply uses:
quiz.explain: SSE is one-way server->client over plain HTTP, ideal for token streams.

quiz.prompt: Where should session state live if API servers are stateless, and what is the trade-off?
rubric: In a shared store: Redis/DB, or client-side signed tokens (JWT/cookies).
Trade-off: extra network hop/latency and a dependency vs freedom to scale/replace servers.
Mentions sticky sessions as a weaker alternative.

practice.title: Index a slow query
practice.brief: No-card path: Postgres in Docker. Generate 1M rows (generate_series), run a filtered + sorted query, capture `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` before and after adding a composite index. Then write half a page: read replicas or sharding for a 95%-read workload at 5k QPS?
practice.done_when: QUERY.md shows both plans (Seq Scan -> Index Scan/Bitmap) with execution times, and the decision note names replication lag and read-your-writes as the main risk.

quiz.prompt: Read replicas mainly help:
options: Read throughput, at the cost of replication lag
quiz.explain: Writes still go to the leader; followers serve reads that may be slightly stale.

quiz.prompt: Consistent hashing minimises:
options: Keys remapped when nodes join or leave
quiz.explain: Only ~K/N keys move instead of nearly all with mod-N hashing.

quiz.prompt: During a network partition, CAP forces a choice between:
quiz.explain: Partition tolerance is not optional in distributed systems.

quiz.prompt: Why is 'read-your-own-writes' hard with asynchronous replicas, and how do you get it?
rubric: The write lands on the leader; the next read may hit a follower that has not applied it.
Fixes: read from leader for a window after a write, session stickiness, or wait for replica LSN/version.
Mentions the cost (leader load) of the fix.

practice.title: Cache-aside with stampede protection
practice.brief: No-card path: Redis in Docker. Add cache-aside to an expensive endpoint (sleep 300 ms) with a 60 s TTL. Add a lock (SET NX PX) so only one request recomputes on a miss. Load it with `hey -c 50`.
practice.done_when: README table of p50/p95 before vs after caching, plus a test showing 50 concurrent misses produce exactly 1 recompute (counter in logs).

quiz.prompt: In cache-aside, on a cache miss the application:
options: Reads the DB, then populates the cache
quiz.explain: The app owns both lookups; the cache is populated lazily.

quiz.prompt: A TTL alone guarantees:
quiz.explain: Data can be stale for at most the TTL.

quiz.prompt: A cache stampede happens when:
options: Many requests miss the same hot key at once and all hit the DB
quiz.explain: Mitigate with locks/single-flight, early refresh or jittered TTLs.

quiz.prompt: What should you NOT cache in an LLM application, and why?
rubric: Personalised/tenant-specific answers under a shared key (data leakage).
Responses from non-deterministic or tool-calling/side-effecting requests.
Answers depending on fast-changing data unless TTL matches freshness.

practice.title: Document-processing jobs that survive crashes
practice.brief: No-card path: Redis + RQ (or arq/Celery) in Compose. POST /jobs returns 202 + job_id; a worker processes it with retries (3, exponential backoff + jitter) and a DLQ; an Idempotency-Key header deduplicates submissions. Kill the worker mid-job.
practice.done_when: Test script submits the same request twice with one key -> one job; after `docker kill worker` + restart the job completes exactly once (one output row); a poisoned job lands in the DLQ after 3 tries.

quiz.prompt: With at-least-once delivery, consumers must be:
quiz.explain: Duplicates will happen; processing twice must have the same effect as once.

quiz.prompt: Exponential backoff with jitter prevents:
quiz.explain: Randomising delays spreads retries out instead of hammering together.

quiz.prompt: Kafka differs from a classic work queue because messages:
options: Persist in an ordered, partitioned log that consumers replay by offset
quiz.explain: Retention + offsets let many consumer groups read independently and replay.

quiz.prompt: When should an API return 202 Accepted instead of 200 OK? Describe what the client does next.
rubric: When work is accepted but not completed (async/long-running).
Response includes a job id/status URL; client polls or receives a webhook.
Mentions idempotency for retries of the submission.

practice.title: Token-bucket middleware
practice.brief: No-card path: local Redis. FastAPI middleware implementing a token bucket per API key in a Lua script (atomic). Return 429 with Retry-After. Add a 2 s timeout + simple circuit breaker on a downstream call.
practice.done_when: A burst test (e.g. 30 requests in 1 s at 10 rps, bucket 20) yields 20 x 200 then 429s with Retry-After; two app replicas share limits (proven by alternating requests); circuit opens after N downstream failures and returns a fallback.

quiz.prompt: A token bucket allows:
options: Bursts up to the bucket size, then a steady refill rate
quiz.explain: Capacity sets the burst; refill rate sets sustained throughput.

quiz.prompt: The right HTTP status for 'rate limited' is:
quiz.explain: 429 Too Many Requests, ideally with Retry-After.

quiz.prompt: A circuit breaker:
options: Fails fast after repeated downstream failures, then probes for recovery
quiz.explain: Closed -> open -> half-open states protect the caller and the dependency.

quiz.prompt: Why must a distributed limiter use atomic operations (Lua script or INCR), not read-then-write?
rubric: Concurrent replicas can read the same count and both allow (race condition).
Atomic script makes check-and-decrement one operation in Redis.
Mentions clock/TTL handling inside the same atomic step.

capstone.title: Design, then prove one slice
capstone.brief: Write two design docs: one classic (e.g. a notification service) and one LLM (multi-tenant RAG assistant). Each needs requirements, estimates, a diagram, data model, scaling plan, failure modes and costs. Then implement one critical slice of the LLM design: a gateway with quotas + cache + fallback, OR a vector-search tier with a measured recall/latency curve. Load-test it and record a 10-minute walkthrough. No-card path: everything runs in Docker locally; hosted models only via free tiers.

levels: Numbers drive choices; assumptions stated; 10x-wrong sensitivity noted
>=3 explicit alternatives rejected with reasons (e.g. pgvector vs Qdrant, sync vs batch)
Rate limits, retries/idempotency, failure modes and a degradation plan covered
Slice measured (p50/p95, recall, cache hit rate, cost) and numbers match the doc
A reviewer unfamiliar with the project can explain the design back after the walkthrough
